docs.text: HardFOC driver PF1550 Driver ¶ A header-only C++20 driver for the NXP PF1550 power management IC. It identifies the chip, applies board power profiles, sets rail voltages and the USB input limit, reads OTP, and reports rail state and faults, on any MCU with I2C. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: identify the chip, apply a profile, set rails, read status, take a diagnostic snapshot, handle faults and read OTP. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with Driver standing for pf1550::PF1550<MyI2c> . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ One PF1550<Bus> object per PMIC, constructed from a pointer to your port and the 7-bit address (default kDefaultI2cAddress , 0x08). Every member returns bool (or fills an out-parameter) and never throws. A false also sets a bit in the sticky error flags, which stay set until you clear them. Task Members Identify EnsureInitialized() , IsInitialized() , ReadDeviceId() , VerifyDevice() , GetI2cAddress() Profiles ApplyProfile(span) , ApplyPortentaH7DefaultProfile() , ApplyPortentaH7CarrierProfile() Rails and limits SetSwVoltageMv() , SetSwVoltage() , SetLdoVoltage() , SetVbusCurrentLimitMa() , SetSwDvsEnabled() Strap pins SetPowerMode() , SetUsbRails() Status ReadPmicStatus() , ReadPmicState() , ReadChargerState() , ReadInterruptCategory() Faults and interrupts ReadLatchedFaults() , ClearLatchedFaults() , SetInterruptMaskAll() Diagnostics ReadDiagnosticSnapshot() , RefreshStatusSnapshot() , RunPowerSelfTest() OTP and raw access ReadOtpByte() , ReadOtpRegion() , ReadRegister() , WriteRegister() Errors GetErrorFlags() , ClearErrorFlags(mask) , GetDriverVersion() Identify the chip ¶ if ( ! pmic . EnsureInitialized ()) { const uint16_t err = pmic . GetErrorFlags (); if ( err & static_cast < uint16_t > ( Driver :: Error :: WrongDeviceId )) { std :: printf ( "not a PF1550 at 0x%02X 
 " , pmic . GetI2cAddress ()); } else { std :: printf ( "no answer at 0x%02X (errors 0x%04X) 
 " , pmic . GetI2cAddress (), err ); } return false ; } EnsureInitialized() brings your bus up, reads DEVICE_ID and accepts only 0x7C. After the first success it returns true without touching the bus. The other members do not require it, but call it first so a wiring problem shows up as DeviceNotFound rather than as a failed rail write. Apply a profile ¶ pmic . SetPowerMode ( pf1550 :: PowerMode :: Run ); // STANDBY strap low pmic . SetUsbRails ( true , true ); // USB_VBUS_EN, USB_OTG_EN high if ( ! pmic . ApplyPortentaH7CarrierProfile ()) { // 23 writes, SW1 first, LDO2_CTRL last return false ; // stopped at the first write that failed } A profile is applied in table order, waiting each entry's delay_us through your port's DelayUs() . It stops at the first write that fails and sets Error::ProfileApply ; the writes before it have already taken effect. Portenta H7 profiles lists every write of the built-in tables; Configuration shows how to write your own. Set rails and limits ¶ bool ok = true ; ok &= pmic . SetLdoVoltage ( 2 , pf1550 :: LdoVoltageCode :: V1_8 ); // LDO2_VOLT = 0x00 pmic . SetSwDvsEnabled ( 2 , true ); // this part's SW2 runs with DVS ok &= pmic . SetSwVoltageMv ( 2 , 1200 ); // SW2_VOLT = 0x30 (0.6 V + 48 x 12.5 mV) ok &= pmic . SetVbusCurrentLimitMa ( 500 ); // VBUS_INLIM_CNFG = 0x70 ok &= pmic . WriteRegister ( pf1550 :: Register :: Sw2Ctrl , pf1550 :: SwCtrlBits :: kEn | pf1550 :: SwCtrlBits :: kStbyEn ); SetLdoVoltage(n, code) writes the RUN set point of LDO n (1 to 3). SetSwVoltageMv(n, mv) and SetSwVoltage(n, code) set the RUN voltage of SW1 or SW2, and only when that buck runs with DVS enabled (declared with SetSwDvsEnabled() ): they write the DVS code for the voltage. They refuse with Error::InvalidParam , writing nothing, for SW3 and for a DVS-disabled SW1 / SW2, whose voltage registers are read-only, and for a voltage that is not on the DVS grid (0.6 V to 1.3875 V in 12.5 mV steps). Any other index is rejected the same way. Enables have no helper: build the control byte from SwCtrlBits or LdoCtrlBits and use WriteRegister() . SwVoltageCode names a voltage SwVoltageCode values are DVS-disabled codes. SetSwVoltage() uses the voltage the code stands for ( V1_1 is 1.1 V) and converts it to the DVS encoding, so codes above 1.3875 V are refused. Rails and OTP has both tables. Read status ¶ pf1550 :: PmicState state {}; pf1550 :: ChargerState charger {}; uint8_t category = 0 ; if ( ! pmic . ReadPmicState ( state ) || ! pmic . ReadChargerState ( charger ) || ! pmic . ReadInterruptCategory ( category )) { return false ; } std :: printf ( "%s, charger %s, INT_CATEGORY 0x%02X 
 " , pf1550 :: PmicStateName ( state ), pf1550 :: ChargerStateName ( charger ), category ); ReadPmicState() decodes STATE_INFO (0x67) into PmicState : Wait , Run , Standby , Sleep , RegsDisable or Unknown . ReadChargerState() decodes CHG_SNS (0x87) into ChargerState (pre-charge, fast charge CC / CV, end of charge, done, faults, off) and can return the raw byte too. PmicStateName() , ChargerStateName() and RailName() give log-friendly strings. Read a diagnostic snapshot ¶ pf1550 :: DiagnosticSnapshot snap {}; if ( ! pmic . ReadDiagnosticSnapshot ( snap )) { // about 30 reads: identity, rails, faults return false ; // fields that were read are still filled in } for ( size_t i = 0 ; i < static_cast < size_t > ( pf1550 :: RailId :: Vsnvs ); ++ i ) { const auto & r = snap . rails [ i ]; std :: printf ( "%-4s %4u mV run=%d stby=%d fault=%d 
 " , pf1550 :: RailName ( static_cast < pf1550 :: RailId > ( i )), r . set_voltage_mv , r . enabled_run , r . enabled_stby , r . stat_latched ); } // Between full reads, refresh only what changes on its own (about 14 reads). return pmic . RefreshStatusSnapshot ( snap ); DiagnosticSnapshot holds identity (DEVICE_ID, OTP_FLAVOR, SILICON_REV), INT_CATEGORY, the decoded state and charger state, VBUS sense, the decoded VBUS input limit, the aggregated FaultFlags , and one RailDiagnostics per rail: raw control and voltage bytes, set point in mV, RUN and STANDBY enables, latched and live fault marks. The VSNVS entry holds the raw VSNVS_CTRL byte, 3000 mV and both enables set: VSNVS is a fixed, always-on output. When a read fails, read_ok is false and Error::DiagnosticRead is set, but every field that was read is kept for logging. RefreshStatusSnapshot() re-reads only what changes without a register write (interrupts, state, charger, VBUS, faults), at about half the bus time of a full read. A monitor polling at 20 Hz can do a full read once a second and refreshes in between. Handle errors and faults ¶ uint8_t category = 0 ; if ( ! pmic . ReadInterruptCategory ( category )) { return false ; } if ( category != 0 ) { // something latched since the last clear pf1550 :: FaultFlags faults {}; if ( ! pmic . ReadLatchedFaults ( faults )) { return false ; } if ( faults . Has ( pf1550 :: FaultFlags :: kLdo2Fault )) { std :: printf ( "LDO2 current limit 
 " ); } // Handle the cause first, then re-arm: write 1 to every status bit. pmic . ClearLatchedFaults (); } Signal Meaning Where to look A call returns false NACK, bad argument or a failed read GetErrorFlags() : I2cWrite , I2cRead , InvalidParam , DeviceNotFound , WrongDeviceId , NotInitialized , ProfileApply , DiagnosticRead , SelfTestFailed INT_CATEGORY non-zero A group has a latched interrupt ReadLatchedFaults() , or the STAT register with ReadRegister() INTB low An unmasked interrupt is pending Masks power up set: SetInterruptMaskAll(false) unmasks every group kVbusInval in FaultFlags VBUS_VALID_SNS is clear: no valid USB or adapter input Expected on battery; ranked kInfo STAT bits are write-1-to-clear: ClearLatchedFaults() writes 0xFF to every STAT register. Clear after you have handled the cause; a bit that comes back at once means the cause is still there. The sticky driver flags are separate: ClearErrorFlags() clears them. ReadLatchedFaults() decodes the STAT registers at the data sheet's bit positions ( Register map ). PWRUP_I and PWRDN_I (a finished RUN / STANDBY / SLEEP transition) are events, not faults, and have no FaultFlags bit; read MISC_INT_STAT0 if you need them. kWdiAssert and kResetBmcu are never set: the PF1550 has no such interrupt bits. Run the boot self-test ¶ pf1550 :: SelfTestResult result {}; const bool pass = pmic . RunPowerSelfTest ( result ); std :: printf ( "self-test %s, worst %s 
 " , pass ? "PASS" : "FAIL" , pf1550 :: FaultSeverityName ( result . worst_severity )); RunPowerSelfTest() takes a full snapshot and passes only when DEVICE_ID is 0x7C, the PMIC is in RUN, every SW and LDO rail is enabled in RUN and no latched fault ranks above kInfo . The ranking is FaultSeverityPortentaH7() : it assumes the Portenta H7's wiring (MCU on SW3, LDO1 and LDO3 critical). On another board, rank result.faults yourself. Read OTP and raw registers ¶ uint8_t otp [ pf1550 :: OtpRegion :: kEndExclusive - pf1550 :: OtpRegion :: kStart ] = {}; if ( ! pmic . ReadOtpRegion ( otp , sizeof otp )) { // 0x1C..0x36, about 2 ms per byte return false ; } uint8_t flavor = 0 ; pmic . ReadRegister ( pf1550 :: Register :: OtpFlavor , flavor ); // 0x00: OTP not burned (A0EP) ReadOtpByte() writes the three unlock keys, the OTP address to FMRADDR, waits 2 ms with DelayUs() and reads FMRDATA. ReadOtpRegion() repeats it and refuses addresses past 0x36. ReadRegister() and WriteRegister() take any pf1550::Register ; the Register map lists them.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one call reaches the chip. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one PF1550 object per PMIC. Its public operations (listed from inc/pf1550.hpp) read and write the PF1550's registers: identification, named register sequences (profiles), rail set points, strap pins, OTP, interrupts and diagnostics. The communication interface (pf1550::BusInterface in inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base: four methods are required, DelayUs() has a default. The platform port is the only code you write. Below it is the chip. Drawn from: inc/pf1550.hpp PF1550 public members ; inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp BusInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer Where Depends on You change it when Hardware-agnostic core : PF1550<Bus> inc/pf1550.hpp , src/pf1550.ipp The interface's methods only Never, for a new board Communication interface : BusInterface<Self> inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp Four methods of your port Never Platform port : your class Your project Your SDK Once per MCU or board ( Porting ) Board knowledge sits beside the core as data, not code: the register sequences in pf1550_profiles.hpp and the Portenta H7 fault-severity table in pf1550_diagnostics.hpp . A board that is not a Portenta H7 passes its own table to ApplyProfile() and classifies faults its own way. Everything above the port is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the unit-test model. That is how the host tests run the real driver code without hardware. How one call reaches the chip ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant D as PF1550 core participant P as Your port participant C as PF1550 A->>D: SetVbusCurrentLimitMa(1500) D->>D: 1500 mA to code 0x14, byte 0xA0 D->>P: Write(0x08, 0x94, [0xA0], 1) P->>C: START 0x08+W 0x94 0xA0 STOP C-->>P: ACK P-->>D: true D-->>A: true A NACK makes the port return false ; the core then sets Error::I2cWrite in its sticky error flags and returns false to the application. Design choices ¶ CRTP, not virtual functions. The interface is a class template parameter. The compiler sees your port's methods directly and inlines them; the driver has no vtable and needs no RTTI. The driver type names the port: PF1550<MyI2c> . No heap, no exceptions. Every member is noexcept . Results come back as bool plus out-parameters; the cause of the last failures stays in GetErrorFlags() until you clear it. Profiles are tables. profiles::RegisterWrite is {reg, value, delay_us} . The core applies a table in order and stops at the first failed write, so a profile cannot leave a later rail half-configured without telling you. Codes, not voltages. docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries marked BREAKING need source changes in code that used the affected API. [Unreleased] ¶ Breaking ¶ The bus's DelayUs(uint32_t) hook is required. BusInterface provided a no-op default, so a port without one compiled and the driver's waits were skipped without a trace: the profile delays between writes (the power-sequencing waits, ApplyProfile() ) and the 2 ms wait of ReadOtpByte() / ReadOtpRegion() . The default is gone and PF1550<BusType> rejects a bus without DelayUs() at compile time with "PF1550 bus must provide DelayUs(uint32_t us) ...". Ports that already define it need no change. New trait pf1550::detail::kHasDelayUs<Bus> . Fixed ¶ The ESP32 example bus waited ceil(us / 1 ms) ticks with vTaskDelay() , which returns up to one tick early; it now rounds the tick count up and adds one tick, so a wait is never shorter than asked (the 2 ms OTP wait could be about 1 ms at 1 kHz). Fixed ¶ Breaking (behaviour): the fault decoder reads SW_INT_STAT0/1 (and their SENSE registers), TEMP_INT_STAT0 and MISC_INT_STAT0 at the data sheet's bit positions (Tables 90, 93, 102, 108). A RUN to STANDBY transition no longer reports kVsysLow / kMcuKill ; SW2, SW3 and the 125 °C flag now come from the right bits. SwIntStat0Bits , SwIntStat1Bits , TempIntStat0Bits::kTempShdn and MiscIntStat0Bits changed value; MiscIntStat0Bits::kWdiAssert / kResetBmcu are deprecated and 0 (no such bits), and FaultFlags::kWdiAssert / kResetBmcu are never set. Breaking (behaviour): SetSwVoltage() writes only a DVS-enabled SW1 / SW2 (declared with SetSwDvsEnabled() ), converting the code's voltage to the DVS encoding (Table 31); it refuses SW3 and DVS-disabled bucks, whose voltage registers are read-only (Tables 31, 37), and voltages above 1.3875 V. Breaking (behaviour): the Portenta H7 profiles no longer write the read-only SWx_VOLT , SWx_STBY_VOLT and SWx_SLP_VOLT registers; each table has 14 writes (the array type changed from 23 to 14 entries). VbusLimitRegToMilliamps() returns 0 for the reserved codes 21 to 31 (Table 58) instead of 1600 to 1800 mA. The diagnostic snapshot fills the VSNVS entry (VSNVS_CTRL byte, 3000 mV, always on; Table 127). RunPowerSelfTest() passes on battery: kVbusInval ranks kInfo in FaultSeverityPortentaH7() . cmake --install installs src/pf1550.ipp ; headers now go to include/hf_pf1550/inc/ (the exported target points there). docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and a PF1550, with which bus settings, and the electrical limits that matter to the host. All values here come from the PF1550 data sheet (Rev. 7, 29 September 2021). The PF1550 is the power supply of the board it sits on: when a value here disagrees with your board's schematic, the schematic wins for pin connections and rail assignments. Host interface pins ¶ Pin Signal Direction and notes 2 SDA In / out, open drain; pull up to VDDIO 3 SCL In; pull up to VDDIO 4 VDDIO I/O supply, 1.7 V to 3.3 V: the logic level of every pin here 7 STANDBY In; asserted means STANDBY, polarity from STANDBYINV 9 INTB Out, open drain; low while an unmasked interrupt is pending 10 RESETBMCU Out, open drain; reset for the application processor 6 PWRON In; enable, level or edge sensitive (OTP) 8 ONKEY In; push button, press and long-press interrupts 1 WDI In; watchdog input from the processor Every logic pin's absolute maximum is 3.6 V, ONKEY's 4.8 V. Connect VDDOTP (pin 5) to ground in the application. Strap pins the driver drives ¶ The driver addresses these by name ( pf1550::CtrlPin ) and by state ( GpioSignal::Active / Inactive ) through your port's GpioSet() . Only STANDBY is a PF1550 pin; the USB enables are board signals that the Portenta H7 routes next to it. docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler (the driver uses std::span ): GCC 10+, Clang 12+ or a current MSVC. CMake 3.16 or newer; ESP-IDF v5.4 or v5.5 for the ESP32-C6 examples. No RTOS, heap or exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns bool or a value, and failures also set a sticky error flag. Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-pf1550-driver.git external/hf-pf1550-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-pf1550-driver Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples have their own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ); you do not need it to use the driver. CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-pf1550-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf::pf1550 ) hf::pf1550 is an alias of the hf_pf1550 INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories ( inc/ and the generated version header) and requires C++20 ( cxx_std_20 ), so your target does not need to set either. find_package(hf_pf1550) works after cmake --install : the headers go to include/hf_pf1550/inc/ and the template implementation they include to include/hf_pf1550/src/ , and hf::pf1550 points at the first. Option Default Effect HF_PF1550_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on targets that link the driver HF_PF1550_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host unit tests in tests/ ( Testing and CI ) ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF component wrapper is examples/esp32/components/hf_pf1550/ . Copy that folder into your project's components/ (or point EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at it) and set the HF_PF1550_ROOT cache variable to the driver checkout; the wrapper stops with a clear message when the path is wrong. Your component then declares REQUIRES hf_pf1550 . The wrapper requires the IDF driver component, which the ESP32 reference port uses. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/hf_pf1550_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, install and package export ESP-IDF examples/esp32/components/hf_pf1550/CMakeLists.txt IDF component wrapper over the same settings The version is set once in the settings file and written into pf1550_version.h at configure time. Read it at compile or run time: const char * v = pf1550 :: PF1550 < MyI2c >:: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" The data sheet ¶ NXP's data sheet is not committed. Two scripts fetch it into the git-ignored _local_reference/ folder and regenerate the plain-text register extract from it: ./scripts/fetch_datasheet.sh # _local_reference/datasheet/PF1550.pdf ./scripts/extract_register_reference.sh # docs/datasheet/PF1550-i2c-register-reference.md Next ¶ Quickstart wires the chip and reads its rails; Porting writes the bus interface for your MCU.

docs.text: Portenta H7 profiles ¶ What the two built-in profiles write to an unprogrammed PF1550 on an Arduino Portenta H7 module, in which order, and when to use each. Both profiles are tables in pf1550_profiles.hpp , applied in order by ApplyProfile() . They are written for the MC34PF1550A0EP (unprogrammed OTP) on the Portenta H7. On any other board, write your own table ( Configuration ). Which one ¶ Profile Use it when Default: ApplyPortentaH7DefaultProfile() You want the order of the Portenta's original firmware; SW1 and SW2 turn off in STANDBY Carrier: ApplyPortentaH7CarrierProfile() A carrier board draws +3V3 from the module, or the LDO inputs hang off SW1 Their names for logs are profiles::kPortentaH7DefaultName ( portenta_h7_default ) and profiles::kPortentaH7CarrierName ( portenta_h7_carrier ). The carrier profile differs from the default in three writes: SW1 comes first. SW1_CTRL = 0x0F , then a 5 ms wait, before any LDO register: on the Portenta the LDO inputs are fed from SW1. SW1 stays on in STANDBY. SW1_CTRL = 0x0F instead of 0x01 (on in RUN only). SW2 stays on in STANDBY. SW2_CTRL = 0x0F instead of 0x01 , so the carrier's +3V3 survives a STANDBY transition. Rails on the Portenta H7 ¶ Rail use from the Portenta H7 module schematic. The middle column is the set point: the profiles write the LDO voltages, and the bucks run at their OTP values (SW1 and SW2 in the DVS-disabled table). Rail (schematic) Set point Feeds SW1 (BUCK1, +3V1SW) 3.0 V, OTP code 0x06 USB / ULPI, SDRAM, Ethernet; the LDO inputs SW2 (BUCK2, +VOUT) 3.3 V, OTP code 0x07 Carrier +3V3, JTAG VTref SW3 (BUCK3) 3.3 V, OTP code 0x0F (on the modules read so far) STM32H747, QSPI flash LDO1 1.0 V, code 0x05 MIPI bridge LDO2 1.8 V, code 0x00 MIPI, USB / ULPI LDO3 1.2 V, code 0x09 STM32 DSI, Ethernet PHY No buck voltage writes Neither profile writes SWx_VOLT , SWx_STBY_VOLT or SWx_SLP_VOLT . SW3's are read-only (no DVS), and so are SW1's and SW2's with DVS disabled, which is the case for 3.0 V and 3.3 V set points; on a DVS-enabled buck the Portenta firmware's codes would have meant 0.6875 V. Read the snapshot to see the OTP set points. On a part whose SW1 or SW2 has DVS, set the voltage with SetSwVoltageMv() after the profile. The carrier profile, write by write ¶ The writes, in table order: Register Value Effect SW1_CTRL (0x35) 0x0F On in RUN, STANDBY, SLEEP, low power; then wait 5 ms LDO2_VOLT (0x4F) 0x00 1.8 V LDO1_VOLT (0x4C) 0x05 1.0 V LDO1_CTRL (0x4D) 0x0F On in every mode, low power LDO3_VOLT (0x52) 0x09 1.2 V LDO3_CTRL (0x53) 0x0F On in every mode, low power PWRCTRL0 (0x58) 0x03 STANDBYDLY = 3 , STANDBYINV = 0 : STANDBY high means standby LED_PWM (0x9C) 0x80 LED enabled at 0/32 duty; wait 1 ms LED_CNFG (0x9E) 0x20 LEDOVRD : software owns the LED, so it stays off; wait 1 ms SW3_CTRL1 (0x42) 0x02 SW3 current limit 1.5 A typical; wait 1 ms VBUS_INLIM_CNFG (0x94) 0xA0 VBUS input limit 1500 mA SW2_CTRL (0x3B) 0x0F On in every mode, low power SW3_CTRL (0x41) 0x0F On in every mode, low power LDO2_CTRL (0x50) 0x0F LDO2 on; always the last write LDO2_CTRL is last in both profiles. That order comes from the Portenta's original start-up code, and earlier bring-up notes report I2C trouble when it was written sooner; the data sheet gives no ordering rule for it. Strap pins ¶ Signal (STM32H747 pin) Normal level Driver call PMIC STANDBY (PJ0) Low: RUN SetPowerMode(PowerMode::Run) USB_VBUS_EN (PJ4) High SetUsbRails(true, ...) USB_OTG_EN (PJ6) High SetUsbRails(..., true) PMIC INT (PK0) Input Read by your code The PF1550 sits on I2C1 (PB6 SCL, PB7 SDA) at 0x08. When to apply ¶ Apply the profile early, after the strap pins and before USB or Ethernet start. The PF1550 keeps its registers across an MCU reset, so a profile that was applied once stays in force until the PMIC is powered down; after changing a profile, power the module down completely (USB and battery off) before you judge the result. docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the bus interface for I2C and the strap pins. The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls four methods (and an optional fifth) on a class you derive from pf1550::BusInterface<Self> (in inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp ). The base class uses CRTP: the calls are resolved at compile time, so there are no virtual functions, no vtable and nothing to allocate. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one PF1550 object per PMIC. Its public operations (listed from inc/pf1550.hpp) read and write the PF1550's registers: identification, named register sequences (profiles), rail set points, strap pins, OTP, interrupts and diagnostics. The communication interface (pf1550::BusInterface in inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base: four methods are required, DelayUs() has a default. The platform port is the only code you write. Below it is the chip. Drawn from: inc/pf1550.hpp PF1550 public members ; inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp BusInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract EnsureInitialized() yes Bring the bus up once; return true when it is ready. Called by the driver's EnsureInitialized() and before every profile Write(addr, reg, data, len) yes [addr+W] [reg] [data...] STOP . The driver always sends len = 1 . Return false on a NACK or timeout Read(addr, reg, data, len) yes [addr+W] [reg] , repeated START, [addr+R] , len bytes, STOP. The driver always reads one byte GpioSet(pin, signal) yes Drive CtrlPin::Standby , UsbVbusEn or UsbOtgEn to Active / Inactive ; do nothing for a pin your board does not wire DelayUs(us) yes Block for at least us microseconds (never less: on an RTOS, round the tick count up and add one tick). There is no default; a bus without it fails to compile with "PF1550 bus must provide DelayUs" addr is the 7-bit address; your SDK may want it shifted. The base class also provides GpioSetActive(pin) and GpioSetInactive(pin) , which call your GpioSet() . The port ¶ my_i2c.hpp class MyI2c : public pf1550 :: BusInterface < MyI2c > { public : // Bring the bus up once; the driver calls this before it first talks to the chip. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_i2c_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One register write: [addr+W] [reg] [data] STOP. Return false on a NACK. bool Write ( uint8_t addr , uint8_t reg , const uint8_t * data , size_t len ) noexcept { if ( len != 1 ) { return false ; // the driver writes one register at a time } const uint8_t frame [ 2 ] = { reg , data [ 0 ]}; return platform_i2c_write ( addr , frame , sizeof frame ); } // One register read: [addr+W] [reg] repeated START [addr+R] [data] STOP. bool Read ( uint8_t addr , uint8_t reg , uint8_t * data , size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write_read ( addr , & reg , 1 , data , len ); } // Strap pins wired to the MCU. Active means: STANDBY high (standby), USB enables high. void GpioSet ( pf1550 :: CtrlPin pin , pf1550 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const int gpio = gpioFor ( pin ); if ( gpio >= 0 ) { platform_gpio_write ( gpio , signal == pf1550 :: GpioSignal :: Active ); } } // Required: block for at least `us` microseconds. docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Talk to a PF1550 from your MCU: wire the I2C bus, write a small port class, identify the chip and read its rails. Reading is safe; writing changes the board's supplies This example only reads. The PF1550 powers the board it sits on, often including the MCU that talks to it: a wrong rail write can brown out the processor or over-volt a peripheral. Read the Portenta H7 profiles page before you apply a profile. 1. Wire it ¶ MCU PF1550 Notes I2C SDA SDA (pin 2) Pull up to VDDIO; up to 400 kHz I2C SCL SCL (pin 3) Pull up to VDDIO GPIO out (optional) STANDBY (pin 7) High moves RUN to STANDBY (default polarity) GPIO in (optional) INTB (pin 9) Open drain, active low: pull it up GND GND Common ground The PF1550 answers on I2C once it has VSYS and its I/O supply VDDIO, so the host does not have to be the processor the PMIC supplies: an external jig can configure it first. Hardware has the full pin list and the electrical limits. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the hf::pf1550 CMake target (or add inc/ and the generated pf1550_version.h to your include path and build with C++20). Active means: STANDBY high (standby), USB enables high. void GpioSet ( pf1550 :: CtrlPin pin , pf1550 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const int gpio = gpioFor ( pin ); if ( gpio >= 0 ) { platform_gpio_write ( gpio , signal == pf1550 :: GpioSignal :: Active ); } } // Required: block for at least `us` microseconds. The driver waits through it between profile // writes and for the 2 ms OTP read; a bus without it does not compile. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : static int gpioFor ( pf1550 :: CtrlPin pin ) noexcept { switch ( pin ) { case pf1550 :: CtrlPin :: Standby : return 10 ; // your board's GPIO numbers; -1 = not wired case pf1550 :: CtrlPin :: UsbVbusEn : return 11 ; case pf1550 :: CtrlPin :: UsbOtgEn : return 12 ; default : return -1 ; } } bool ready_ = false ; }; Porting explains each method and the strap-pin levels. 4. Read the rails ¶ main.cpp #include <cstdio> #include "pf1550.hpp" int bring_up_pmic ( MyI2c & bus ) { pf1550 :: PF1550 < MyI2c > pmic ( & bus ); // 7-bit address 0x08 if ( ! pmic . EnsureInitialized ()) { // 1. bus up, DEVICE_ID == 0x7C return -1 ; // wiring, pull-ups or address } pf1550 :: PmicState state {}; // 2. where is the state machine? if ( ! pmic . ReadPmicState ( state ) || state != pf1550 :: PmicState :: Run ) { return -2 ; } pf1550 :: DiagnosticSnapshot snap {}; // 3. SW1..LDO3: set point and enable if ( ! pmic . ReadDiagnosticSnapshot ( snap )) { return -3 ; } for ( size_t i = 0 ; i <= static_cast < size_t > ( pf1550 :: RailId :: Ldo3 ); ++ i ) { const auto id = static_cast < pf1550 :: RailId > ( i ); std :: printf ( "%s %u mV %s \n " , pf1550 :: RailName ( id ), snap . rails [ i ]. set_voltage_mv , snap . rails [ i ]. enabled_run ? "on" : "off" ); } return 0 ; } What each step does: EnsureInitialized() calls your port's EnsureInitialized() , reads DEVICE_ID (register 0x00) and checks it is 0x7C. Later calls return at once. ReadPmicState() decodes STATE_INFO (0x67). Run means the start-up sequence has finished and the OTP-enabled regulators are on. ReadDiagnosticSnapshot() reads about 30 registers: identity, state, charger and VBUS sense, every rail's set point and enables, and the latched faults. This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. docs.text: Rails and OTP ¶ How the PF1550 encodes rail voltages, enables and limits, which registers OTP controls, and what that means for the values the driver writes. All tables come from the PF1550 data sheet , Rev. 7; the driver's decoders in pf1550_voltage_tables.hpp implement them and check themselves at compile time. OTP decides first ¶ At start-up (REGS_DISABLE to RUN) the PF1550 copies its OTP into the regulator registers: set points, enables, sequence, current limits, charger parameters. Register Bits, from bit 0 Meaning INT_CATEGORY (0x06) CHG_INT , SW1_INT , SW2_INT , SW3_INT , LDO_INT , ONKEY_INT , TEMP_INT , MISC_INT A group has a pending interrupt SW_INT_STAT0 (0x08) SW1_LS_I , SW2_LS_I , SW3_LS_I Low-side current limit SW_INT_STAT1 (0x0B) SW1_HS_I , SW2_HS_I , SW3_HS_I High-side current limit SW_INT_STAT2 (0x0E) SW1_DVS_DONE_I , SW2_DVS_DONE_I DVS transition finished LDO_INT_STAT0 (0x18) LDO1_FAULTI , LDO2_FAULTI , LDO3_FAULTI LDO fault TEMP_INT_STAT0 (0x20) THERM110I , unused, THERM125I Die temperature crossed 110 °C / 125 °C MISC_INT_STAT0 (0x28) PWRUP_I , PWRDN_I , PWRON_I , LOW_SYS_WARN_I , SYS_OVLO_I Back in RUN, entered STANDBY / SLEEP, PWRON button, VSYS below LOW_SYS_WARN, VSYS over SYS_OVLO ReadLatchedFaults() maps these bits into FaultFlags : SW1/2/3_LS_I and _HS_I to kSwNLs / kSwNHs , LDOn_FAULTI to kLdoNFault , THERM110I to kTempWarn , THERM125I to kTempShdn , PWRON_I to kPwrOn , LOW_SYS_WARN_I to kVsysLow and SYS_OVLO_I to kVsysOv . PWRUP_I and PWRDN_I are mode-transition events and are not mapped. The SENSE registers use the same layout as their STAT registers.

docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host unit tests against a register model of the chip, compiled documentation, ESP32 builds and static analysis, on every pull request. Host unit tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a mock bus that models a PF1550 at the register level: it answers only at its address, reports DEVICE_ID 0x7C and STATE_INFO RUN, treats the interrupt status registers as write-1-to-clear, models the indirect OTP read behind the three keys, and records every transfer, strap-pin change and delay. cmake -S . -B build-host -DHF_PF1550_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build-host ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_driver.cpp Identification and its errors, profile order and waits, a profile that stops at a failed write, rail and VBUS setters, strap pins, the OTP unlock sequence, fault clearing, the diagnostic snapshot and self-test, the data sheet's code tables tests/test_conformance.cpp Data sheet conformance: interrupt status bit positions (Tables 90, 93, 102, 108), SW voltage writes only on DVS bucks (Tables 31, 37), profiles without read-only writes, reserved VBUS limit codes (Table 58), the VSNVS entry (Table 127), the self-test without VBUS (Table 153) tests/compile_fail/no_delay_hook.cpp.in Must not compile: a bus without DelayUs() . The ctest hf_pf1550_requires_delay_hook passes only when the compiler stops at the driver's static_assert tests/install_check.cmake cmake --install into the build tree, then compile a consumer against the installed headers only tests/mock_pf1550.hpp The register model tests/test_harness.hpp , tests/test_main.cpp A dependency-free test runner Documentation snippets ¶ Every C++ block on this site is included from tests/docs/ , which the host build compiles (target hf_pf1550_doc_snippets , -Wall -Wextra ) with the driver instantiated over the documented port. A change to the API that breaks a page breaks the build first. The README's example is a copy of the Quickstart snippet that hardfoc-docs check keeps in step, and the register table on the Register map page is generated from inc/pf1550_registers.hpp the same way. CI workflows ¶ Workflow What it checks Host unit tests GCC and Clang build and run the tests and the doc snippets ESP32 examples build Every app in examples/esp32/app_config.yml , for each listed ESP-IDF version and build type C++ lint, C++ analysis clang-format, clang-tidy and cppcheck Docs Strict site build, figure and generated-table drift, Doxygen, link check, Lighthouse budget Markdown lint, YAML lint, link check Repository text files The workflows call the shared, versioned workflows of hf-general-ci-tools and hf-espidf-ci-tools . scripts/verify_driver_scaffold.sh is a local check of the repository layout, a CMake configure and the profile table sizes. On hardware ¶ The ESP32 examples are the hardware checks: pf1550_esp32c6_diagnostics runs the self-test at boot and a snapshot every 5 s, and pf1550_esp32c6_provision prints a checklist of the rail voltages to measure. Measuring the rails, USB behaviour and I2C waveforms stays a bench job.

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up a PF1550, their causes and the fix for each, cheapest check first. Start with GetErrorFlags() after a failing call: DeviceNotFound or I2cRead / I2cWrite point at the bus, WrongDeviceId at the device, InvalidParam at the arguments, ProfileApply at a write the chip refused. The chip does not answer ¶ Symptom Cause Fix EnsureInitialized() fails with DeviceNotFound No ACK at 0x08 Check the pull-ups to VDDIO, SDA and SCL not swapped, a common ground Same, and the SDK logs an address of 0x10 8-bit address passed to a 7-bit API Pass 0x08; shift only inside your port if the SDK wants it Same, on a programmed part OTP selects another address (0x09 to 0x0F) Scan the bus and pass the address to the constructor WrongDeviceId Another device answers at 0x08, or DEVICE_ID is not 0x7C Read ReadDeviceId() ; a PF1500 reads 0x78 Errors at high bus speed Clock above 400 kHz, or edges faster than 20 ns Run at 400 kHz or less; lower the master's drive strength The ESP32 example reports no device Nothing wired, or the wrong pins Expected without hardware; otherwise check Kconfig PF1550_I2C_SDA_GPIO / SCL_GPIO Writes do not change the rails ¶ Symptom Cause Fix SetSwVoltage() / SetSwVoltageMv() return false SW3, or an SW1 / SW2 declared DVS-disabled: those voltage registers are read-only. Or the voltage is off the DVS grid Change the set point in OTP, or declare DVS with SetSwDvsEnabled() if the part has it ( Rails and OTP ) A rail reads far below the expected voltage A DVS-disabled code written with WriteRegister() to a DVS-enabled SW1 / SW2 (0x07 is 0.6875 V there) Use SetSwVoltageMv() ; declare the mode with SetSwDvsEnabled() A profile change has no effect after a reset The PMIC kept the previous values: an MCU reset does not reset it Power the PMIC down completely, then apply the profile again The snapshot shows the old values after a profile The profile stopped at a failed write Check the return value and ProfileApply ; the writes before it did happen SetVbusCurrentLimitMa() returns false The value is not 10, 100, 500, 1000 or 1500 mA Write VBUS_INLIM_CNFG with code << 3 for other Table 58 values Board symptoms (Portenta H7 and carriers) ¶ Symptom Cause Fix Carrier +3V3 or JTAG VTref is 0 V while the processor runs SW2 is off; with the default profile it also turns off in STANDBY Apply the carrier profile ( SW2_CTRL = 0x0F ) LDO outputs are dead but the processor runs The LDO inputs hang off SW1, which is not up yet Use the carrier profile: SW1 first, then a 5 ms wait USB does not enumerate after boot USB_VBUS_EN / USB_OTG_EN low, or STANDBY high SetPowerMode(PowerMode::Run) and SetUsbRails(true, true) before USB starts The rails drop when the board idles STANDBY asserted, and the rail's STBY_EN bit is clear Drive STANDBY low, or set kStbyEn in the rail's control register Faults and self-test ¶ Symptom Cause Fix A fault comes back right after ClearLatchedFaults() The cause is still there Read the SENSE register for the live state INTB never goes low Every interrupt is masked (the reset value) SetInterruptMaskAll(false) , or unmask one group What software cannot check ¶ Measure the rails, VBUS / OTG behaviour on USB-C and the I2C waveforms under load with instruments; the snapshot reports set points and status bits, not voltages.

CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Three layers, one of them yours ¶ Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one PF1550 object per PMIC. Its public operations (listed from inc/pf1550.hpp) read and write the PF1550's registers: identification, named register sequences (profiles), rail set points, strap pins, OTP, interrupts and diagnostics. The communication interface (pf1550::BusInterface in inc/pf1550_i2c_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base: four methods are required, DelayUs() has a default. The platform port is the only code you write.
